### Welcome

Today we are going to introduce the topic of hierarchical models following [Chapter 15 of Bayes Rules!](https://www.bayesrulesbook.com/chapter-15) very closely

### Libraries

```{r}
library(bayesrules)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggpubr)
library(rstanarm)
library(broom.mixed)
library(tidybayes)
```

### Data

This data, a subset of the `Cherry` data in the **mdsr** package ([Baumer, Horton, and Kaplan 2021](https://www.bayesrulesbook.com/chapter-15#ref-R-mdsr)), contains the `net` running times (in minutes) for 36 participants in the annual 10-mile Cherry Blossom race held in Washington, D.C.. Each runner is in their 50s or 60s and has entered the race in multiple years.

```{r}
running <- bayesrules::cherry_blossom_sample
```

### Guided Exploratory Viz

We only have a few more chance to practice exploratory viz with `ggplot()` left this semester so do your best to follow these guided questions

1.  What is the general distribution of run times

```{r}
ggplot(running, aes(x = net)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Net time (minutes)", y = "Count")
```

2.  What is the average run time by age

```{r}
running %>%
  dplyr::group_by(age) %>%
  dplyr::summarize(mean_net = mean(net)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = mean_net)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line()
```

3.  What is the distribution of run time by age

```{r}
ggplot(running, aes(x = factor(age), y = net)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Net time (minutes)")
```

4.  Did runner 27 get faster or slower with age?

```{r}
running %>%
  filter(runner == "27") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = net)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

5.  Has the average race time changed over the years

```{r}
running %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(mean_net = mean(net)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_net)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line()
```

6.  What is the distribution of the difference between net and gun

```{r}
running %>%
  mutate(diff = gun - net) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Gun time minus net time (minutes)")
```

7.  What is the distribution of run time by runner

```{r}
ggplot(running, aes(x = reorder(runner, net, median), y = net)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Runner", y = "Net time (minutes)")
```

### Model Question

What is the relationship between age and race time?

```{r}
running <- running %>%
  select(runner, age, net) 
```

#### Complete Pooling

Combine all 252 observations across our 36 runners into *one pool* of information

```{r}
ggplot(running, aes(y = net, x = age)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  stat_cor()
```

Bayesian?

```{r}
complete_pooled_model <- stan_glm(
  net ~ age, 
  data = running, family = gaussian, 
  prior_intercept = normal(0, 2.5, autoscale = TRUE),
  prior = normal(0, 2.5, autoscale = TRUE), 
  prior_aux = exponential(1, autoscale = TRUE),
  chains = 4, iter = 5000*2, seed = 84735)
```

```{r}
tidy(complete_pooled_model, conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.80)
```

This seems a bit strange. Our own experience does not support the idea that we’ll continue to run at the same speed.

```{r}
# Plot of the posterior median model
ggplot(running, aes(x = age, y = net, group = runner)) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "gray", size = 0.5) + 
  geom_abline(aes(intercept = 75.2, slope = 0.268), color = "blue") +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
# Select an example subset
examples <- running %>% 
  filter(runner %in% c("1", "20", "22"))

ggplot(examples, aes(x = age, y = net)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  facet_wrap(~ runner) + 
  geom_abline(aes(intercept = 75.2242, slope = 0.2678), 
              color = "blue")
```

#### No pooling

Having failed with our complete pooled model, let’s swing to the other extreme. Instead of lumping everybody together into one pool and ignoring any information about runners, the **no pooling** approach considers each of our m=36 runners *separately*.

```{r}
ggplot(examples, aes(x = age, y = net)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, fullrange = TRUE) + 
  facet_wrap(~ runner) + 
  xlim(52, 62)
```

Based on the no pooling results for our three example cases, what do you anticipate your running times to be? Are you stumped? If not, you should be. The no pooling approach can’t help you answer this question. Since they’re tailored to the 36 individuals in our sample, the resulting 36 models don’t reliably extend beyond these individuals.

### Partial Pooling with hierarchical models

```{r}
running_model_1 <- stan_glmer(
  net ~ age + (1 | runner), 
  data = running, family = gaussian,
  prior_intercept = normal(100, 10),
  prior = normal(2.5, 1), 
  prior_aux = exponential(1, autoscale = TRUE),
  prior_covariance = decov(reg = 1, conc = 1, shape = 1, scale = 1),
  chains = 4, iter = 5000*2, seed = 84735)
```

- **`net ~ age`**: on average, race time changes in a straight line with age, with slope β₁ (minutes per year).

- **`(1 | runner)`**: each runner gets their own baseline shift b_j. Some runners are consistently faster than average at a given age and some consistently slower. Repeated races by the same person are therefore treated as related, not independent. The b_j values come from a common normal distribution with standard deviation σ_b, which is what lets the model share information across runners.

- **`family = gaussian`**: the leftover race-to-race variation within a runner is normal, with standard deviation σ_y.

**The priors, which are the assumptions you state before seeing the data.**

- **`prior_intercept = normal(100, 10)`**: before seeing data, you expect the typical runner’s race time to be about 100 minutes, give or take 10 minutes. `rstanarm` centers the predictors, so this is the time at the average age.

- **`prior = normal(2.5, 1)`**: you expect each additional year of age to add about 2.5 minutes, give or take 1, so slopes from about 0.5 to 4.5 minutes per year are plausible.

- **`prior_aux = exponential(1, autoscale = TRUE)`**: this is the prior on σ_y, the within-runner noise. It favors smaller values, and `autoscale = TRUE` rescales it to the spread of the data, so you aren’t setting units by hand.

- **`prior_covariance = decov(reg = 1, conc = 1, shape = 1, scale = 1)`**: this is the prior on how much runners differ from each other (σ_b). With a single random intercept, there is only one standard deviation, so the extra settings mostly don’t matter. It amounts to a gentle prior favoring moderate between-runner variation.

**The sampling settings.**

- **`chains = 4`**: four independent runs of the sampler, so you can check that they agree.

- **`iter = 5000*2`**: each chain runs 10,000 iterations. The first half is warmup and is discarded, leaving 5,000 draws per chain and 20,000 in total.

- **`seed = 84735`**: makes the results reproducible

```{r}
tidy_summary_1 <- tidy(running_model_1, effects = "fixed",
                       conf.int = TRUE, conf.level = 0.80)
tidy_summary_1

```

There’s an 80% chance that the *typical* runner tends to slow down somewhere between 1.02 and 1.58 minutes per year

```{r}
# Posterior summaries of runner-specific intercepts
runner_summaries_1 <- running_model_1 %>%
  spread_draws(`(Intercept)`, b[,runner]) %>% 
  mutate(runner_intercept = `(Intercept)` + b) %>% 
  select(-`(Intercept)`, -b) %>% 
  median_qi(.width = 0.80) %>% 
  select(runner, runner_intercept, .lower, .upper)
```

```{r}
tidy(running_model_1, effects = "ran_pars")
```

```{r}
B0 <- tidy_summary_1$estimate[1]
B1 <- tidy_summary_1$estimate[2]
running %>%
  select(runner, age, net) %>%      # only the variables in the model
  drop_na() %>%
  add_epred_draws(running_model_1, ndraws = 200, re_formula = NA) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = net)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .epred, group = .draw), alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_abline(intercept = B0, slope = B1, color = "blue") +
  lims(y = c(75, 110))
```

### Takeaway

Pooling all runners’ data together masks the fact that most *individual* runners slow down with age. Hierarchical models with varying intercepts allow us to quantify this relationship more effectively

### Exercise Questions:

Use the [text](https://www.bayesrulesbook.com/chapter-15) to answer these questions:\
Can you give me an example when we might want to use the partial pooling approach?

1.  Why wouldn’t we always just use the complete pooling approach? It seems easier.

    If you treat all 252 races as independent, you ignore the fact that some runners appear more than once. When you overlook that, you miss important patterns within each runner and you can easily draw the wrong conclusions. The pooled model spits out a slope of just 0.27 minutes per year, with an 80% interval that runs from -0.30 to 0.84. Since that interval includes zero, the model is basically saying runners don’t slow down with age, even though most runners do. \
    \
    Now, compare that to the partial pooling model. This one estimates a much steeper slope 1.30 minutes per year with a tighter 80% interval from 1.02 to 1.58. Plus, the standard error shrinks to about half (0.22 instead of 0.45) since the model actually recognizes that differences between runners are real, not just noise. Sure, complete pooling is simpler, but it often misses the real story.

2.  Does the no pooled approach have any drawbacks? It seems that there are fewer assumptions.

    It doesn’t assume much about how runners compare to each other, but that’s actually a big downside. Every runner gets their own model, built from just a handful of races like five times out on the track so the numbers are all over the place. One runner might end up with a negative slope, meaning they actually get faster as they age (which doesn’t make sense), while another has a crazy steep positive slope, slowing way down. If you use these personalized models to guess each runner’s race time at age 62, you get stuff like 63 minutes for one person and 146 minutes for another. Those predictions just don’t add up.

    Since each model fits only those 36 runners, none of them help you predict what someone new might do, or what the average runner looks like. By ignoring the fact that these runners have things in common like how people in their 50s and 60s usually slow down you lose valuable information they all share.

3.  Can you remind me what the difference is between *within-group* variability and *between-group* variability? And how does that relate to partial pooling?

Within-group variability just means how much a runner’s times jump around from race to race, compared to their usual time. That’s σ_y. Between-group variability is about how much runners differ from each other so it measures the spread in their baseline speeds (σ_b). In this dataset, you see typical times for different runners going from about 63 up to 118 minutes. But each runner’s times stick pretty close to their own average. So, runners are more different from each other than they are inconsistent within themselves.

Partial pooling tries to find a middle ground. Each runner’s estimate blends their own race data with the overall average, and statisticians call this “shrinkage.” If runners aren’t that different so between-group variability is low compared to within-group variability then everyone’s estimates get pulled closer to the average, kind of like fully pooling them together. If runners really do have their own distinct speeds so between-group variability is high then each runner’s estimate stays much closer to their personal data, like no pooling at all. And if a runner doesn’t have much data, their estimate gets pulled in even more.
